claim: To extend an existing Active Directory to AWS, AWS Managed Microsoft AD connects to it with Active Directory trusts so users keep their on-premises credentials without synchronizing users, groups or passwords; alternatively, the on-premises domain can be migrated to AWS Managed Microsoft AD with the Active Directory Migration Toolkit (ADMT) and the Password Export Service.
question: How can AWS Managed Microsoft AD work with an existing on-premises Active Directory, and how can the domain be migrated?

values.display: synchronize users, groups, or passwords
Active Directory Migration Toolkit (ADMT)

qualifiers.scope: AWS Managed Microsoft AD with an existing Active Directory

evidence.quote: This means your users can access Active Directory-aware and AWS applications with their on-premises Active Directory credentials, without needing you to synchronize users, groups, or passwords.

You can also migrate your on-premises Active Directory domain to AWS to be free of the operational burden of your Active Directory infrastructure using the [Active Directory Migration Toolkit (ADMT)](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-migrate-your-on-premises-domain-to-aws-managed-microsoft-ad-using-admt/) along with the Password Export Service (PES) to perform the migration.

claim: Directory members have no access to AWS resources by default; to give them AWS Management Console access you assign IAM roles to directory users or groups, and the directory must have an access URL.
question: How do Active Directory users sign in to the AWS Management Console through AWS Managed Microsoft AD?

values.display: do not have access to any AWS resources
You assign IAM roles to your directory members
your directory must have an access URL

qualifiers.scope: AWS Management Console access with AWS Managed Microsoft AD credentials

evidence.quote: By default, your directory members do not have access to any AWS resources. You assign IAM roles to your directory members to give them access to the various AWS services and resources.
Before you can grant console access to your directory members, your directory must have an access URL.

claim: MFA for AWS Managed Microsoft AD requires an MFA solution that is a RADIUS server, or an MFA plugin to a RADIUS server in your infrastructure; the directory's RADIUS client sends the username and OTP code to the RADIUS server before authenticating the user against Active Directory.
question: What does AWS Managed Microsoft AD need to enable MFA?

values.display: (RADIUS) server
includes a RADIUS client

evidence.quote: To enable MFA, you must have an MFA solution that is a [Remote authentication dial-in user service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RADIUS) (RADIUS) server, or you must have an MFA plugin to a RADIUS server already implemented in your on-premises infrastructure.

AWS Managed Microsoft AD includes a RADIUS client that connects to the RADIUS server upon which you have implemented your MFA solution. Your RADIUS server validates the username and OTP code. If your RADIUS server successfully validates the user, AWS Managed Microsoft AD then authenticates the user against Active Directory.

claim: A Cognito identity pool is a directory of federated identities that can be exchanged for AWS credentials; it accepts an ID or access token, a user pool token, a SAML assertion or a social-provider OAuth token, and users can start as guests and sign in later to unlock more access.
question: What can a Cognito identity pool exchange for AWS credentials?

values.display: a directory of federated identities
a SAML assertion, or a social-provider OAuth token
Users can start out as guests

evidence.quote: An Amazon Cognito identity pool is a directory of federated identities that you can exchange for AWS credentials.
Exchange an ID or access token, a user pool token, a SAML assertion, or a social-provider OAuth token for AWS credentials.
Users can start out as guests and retrieve assets that you keep in AWS services.

claim: Identity pools have two authentication flows with public providers, enhanced and basic; in the enhanced flow the app calls GetId and then GetCredentialsForIdentity, the identity pool handles IAM role selection (default role, RBAC or ABAC), and the AWS credentials are valid for one hour; in the basic flow the application selects the IAM role.
question: What is the difference between the enhanced and basic identity pool flows, and how long are enhanced-flow credentials valid?

values.display: enhanced and basic
valid for one hour
your application selects the IAM role

evidence.quote: Amazon Cognito has two different flows for authentication with public providers: enhanced and basic.

Enhanced authentication manages the logic of IAM role selection and credentials retrieval in your identity pool configuration. You can configure your identity pool to select a default role, to apply attribute-based access control (ABAC) or role-based access control (RBAC) principles to role selection. The AWS credentials from enhanced authentication are valid for one hour.
When you implement the basic authentication flow, your application selects the IAM role that you want users to assume.

claim: Revoking a refresh token invalidates all access tokens issued from it; GlobalSignOut (authorized by the user's access token) and AdminUserGlobalSignOut (authorized by an administrator's IAM credentials) revoke all of a user's refresh, ID and access tokens; revoked JWTs still pass a check by any JWT library that only verifies signature and expiration.
question: How can Cognito user pool tokens be revoked, and does revocation stop a JWT that is verified locally?

values.display: issued by that refresh token become invalid
target user's refresh, ID, and access tokens
revoked tokens will still be valid

qualifiers.condition: token revocation enabled on the app client

evidence.quote: When you revoke a refresh token, all access tokens that were previously issued by that refresh token become invalid.

[AdminUserGlobalSignOut](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito-user-identity-pools/latest/APIReference/API_AdminUserGlobalSignOut.html) is a server-side operation that an administrator authorizes with IAM credentials. This operation revokes all of the target user's refresh, ID, and access tokens.

Revoked tokens can't be used with any Amazon Cognito API calls that require a token. However, revoked tokens will still be valid if they are verified using any JWT library that verifies the signature and expiration of the token.

claim: Token revocation is enabled by default when a new user pool app client is created, and refresh tokens can be revoked only in app clients with token revocation enabled.
question: Is token revocation on by default for a new Cognito app client?

values.display: token revocation is enabled by default
only in app clients with token revocation enabled

qualifiers.scope: per Cognito user pool app client

evidence.quote: + When you create a new user pool client, token revocation is enabled by default.
+ You can revoke refresh tokens only in app clients with token revocation enabled.

claim: An Application Load Balancer can authenticate users before they reach the application, through an OIDC-compliant IdP or through Cognito user pools (social IdPs and corporate SAML, OIDC or OAuth identities); the authenticate-cognito and authenticate-oidc actions are supported only on HTTPS listeners.
question: Can an ALB authenticate users with a Cognito user pool, and which listener protocol does it need?

values.display: offload the work of authenticating users
supported only with HTTPS listeners

evidence.quote: You can configure an Application Load Balancer to securely authenticate users as they access your applications. This enables you to offload the work of authenticating users to your load balancer so that your applications can focus on their business logic.
The `authenticate-cognito` and `authenticate-oidc` action types are supported only with HTTPS listeners.
+ Authenticate users through corporate identities, using SAML, OpenID Connect (OIDC), or OAuth, through the user pools supported by Amazon Cognito.
